entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize time invariance by interpreting whether delaying or advancing any continuous-time input causes the system output to undergo the identical delay or advance without changing shape or rule.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Meaning of Time Invariance
sections.learning_goal: Define time invariance for a continuous-time system as exact commutation with input shifts and express the criterion in a single equation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visuals needed for this symbolic definition lesson.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the single test condition: replace x(t) with x(t-T), compute both shift-then-system and system-then-shift outputs, and require equality for all t and T before declaring invariance.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a minimal delay example with a memoryless system y(t)=x(t) and shift parameter T as a concrete anchor.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the distinction between delaying/advancing the input first versus delaying/advancing the output after the system and why both must match.
Define shorthand for the two paths: TTS (time-shift then system) and STS (system then shift) with explicit notation.
State the invariance test rule: a system is time invariant iff TTS and STS are identical for arbitrary x(t) and arbitrary T.
Identify the practical failure checks: same shift direction, same shift magnitude, same signal rule and shape after substitution.
Preview the three worked examples: matching delay, matching advance, and a mismatch case where pattern changes.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $y(t)=x(t)$, test whether a delay of $T$ in the input yields the same output delay.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show both paths and verify exact equality to establish a canonical time-invariant base case.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first worked example and sets the base symbolic template for later sections.
solution_step_plan: Compute the shifted input path: x_1(t)=x(t-T)$ and then y_{tts}(t)=x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.
Compute the direct path: y(t)=x(t)$, then form y_{sts}(t)=y(t-T)=x(t-T)$.
Compare the two expressions and conclude they are identical for all t,T.
Classify this system as time invariant and explicitly name the invariant feature (rule unchanged, shape unchanged, shift preserved).
practice_variation_axes: use a generic arbitrary system rule instead of identity
substitute symbolic T and then a numeric T example
require recognizing commutation without computing full signal forms

sections.handoff_notes: Use the tutorial as a strict minimum-dose direct-instruction block followed by worked examples and deliberate practice; keep algebra light and reusable so questions are generated cleanly.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Delay
sections.learning_goal: Train recognition of time invariance when the input delay produces the same delayed output under a nontrivial system rule.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No signal plot needed; algebraic substitution is sufficient.

question_policy.answer_format: Algebraic comparisons of two expressions
question_policy.practice_question_model: For y(t)=2x(t-1), test whether y_{tts}(t) and y_{sts}(t) match for delay x(t-T).
distractor_plan: Include a distractor where shift direction is flipped incorrectly (using x(t+T) in one path).
Include a distractor that checks only one side simplification and misses TTS vs STS substitution order.
Include a distractor where parameter T is accidentally treated as a fixed number instead of arbitrary.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test time invariance for $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ under input delay $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the delay propagates through the system unchanged even with a fixed delay offset inside x(t-1).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds a fixed internal delay to the system rule while preserving output delay equivalence.
solution_step_plan: Form TTS: substitute x_1(t)=x(t-T) into y(t), giving $y_{tts}(t)=2x((t)-1-T)=2x(t-T-1)$.
Form STS: compute $y(t)=2x(t-1)$ then delay output: $y_{sts}(t)=2x((t-T)-1)=2x(t-T-1)$.
Compare both expressions term-by-term and mark them identical.
Conclude this system is time invariant and note the fixed offset does not break shift commutation.
practice_variation_axes: multiply-by-constant coefficient changes
replace -1 shift constant with +1 and keep the same delay test
swap T from symbolic to numeric while preserving method

sections.handoff_notes: Focus on a single symbolic control-flow pattern: TTS and STS algebra must be written first, then compared. Keep answer choices consistent with expression-level equality.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Matching Output Advance
sections.learning_goal: Generalize the same invariance check to advance shifts and avoid sign mistakes in substituted-time arguments.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No visual needed; advance vs delay distinction is handled with sign conventions in expressions.

question_policy.answer_format: Symbolic comparisons of shifted arguments
question_policy.practice_question_model: For y(t)=5x(t), check whether delaying the input by T and advancing by T are both handled as the same rule with x(t\pm T).
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that swaps signs between x(t+T) and x(t-T) in one path.
Include a distractor that claims invariance despite mismatched internal argument after substitution.
Include a distractor that fails to apply shift to the whole expression y(t) before comparison.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Test time invariance for $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$ using an advance input $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the path comparison remains equal when handling advance notation correctly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: One meaningful wrinkle: swap delay for advance to verify students track sign conventions while using the same compare-step method.
solution_step_plan: Compute TTS: $x_1(t)=x(t+T)$, then $y_{tts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+T)$.
Compute STS: $y(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)$, then $y_{sts}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t+T)$.
Write the equality line explicitly with matching signs and conclude equality.
Explain why this is still a matched output advance, so the system is time invariant here as well.
practice_variation_axes: replace coefficient and numeric scale
choose advance with a non-identity symbol such as t+2T
test both y(t)=a x(t) and y(t)=b x(t)+c forms

sections.handoff_notes: Keep advance examples explicit and non-ambiguous about whether T shifts right or left; this section should reduce common sign errors before introducing non-invariant forms.

sections.section_title: Recognizing When a Shift Changes the Output Pattern
sections.learning_goal: Identify the non-invariance signature where shifted input does not produce merely shifted output because the output pattern or rule changes.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No plots required; signal-shape change is exposed via algebraic argument form only.

question_policy.answer_format: Short equation-justification choices
question_policy.practice_question_model: For y(t)=t\,x(t), classify whether a delay x(t-T) results in output y(t-T) when using TTS and STS.
distractor_plan: Include a distractor that incorrectly cancels t with t-T by canceling algebraic factors.
Include a distractor that treats t x(t) as if t and T are interchangeable constants.
Include a distractor that compares only one side numerically and misses the mismatch in argument form.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Check whether $y(t)=t\,x(t)$ is time invariant under input shift $x_1(t)=x(t-T)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that explicit time-dependent multiplicative factor alters output pattern, so TTS and STS differ.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Introduces the minimal mismatch pattern change while reusing the exact compare workflow from delay/advance sections.
solution_step_plan: Compute TTS: $y_{tts}(t)=t\,x(t-T)$.
Compute STS: y(t)=t\,x(t)$, then delay output: $y_{sts}(t)=(t-T)x(t-T)$.
Compare: one side is t x(t-T), the other is (t-T) x(t-T); identify mismatch term.
State that the output shape/rule changes, so the system is not time invariant.
practice_variation_axes: change coefficient from t to t^2 and reuse the same mismatch test
swap T with -T and show the same mismatch logic
replace output pattern with t+2 or sin(t) multiplicative terms

Separate signal shifting from any later claim about the system being time invariant.
practice_variation_axes: Shift amount
Delay versus advance
Signal notation used in the prompt
Whether the shifted signal is written as an expression or a short description

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example on one signal only. The follow-up question should test shift recognition, not system comparison.

sections.section_title: Comparing the Shift-Then-System and System-Then-Shift Paths
sections.learning_goal: Carry out the two-path test by computing $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ and comparing it to $y(t-\tau)$ where $y(t)=T\{x(t)\}$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the comparison is purely algebraic.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the option that correctly compares the two output paths and identifies whether they match.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a simple system such as $T\{x(t)\}=x^2(t)$ and a shifted input $x(t-\tau)$, compare $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ with $y(t-\tau)$ and decide whether the paths match.
distractor_plan: Drop the shift inside the system and compare the wrong expressions.
Change the shift direction on one path.
Confuse $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ with $T\{x(t)\}-\tau$.
Treat the system rule as if it shifts the output by itself.
Pick an answer that changes amplitude instead of time.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=x^2(t)$, compare the output for the shifted input $x(t-\tau)$ with the shifted original output $y(t-\tau)$ when $y(t)=T\{x(t)\}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that both paths produce the same expression, so the delay propagates unchanged.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step adds the system-comparison test after the learner already knows how to recognize a shifted signal.
solution_step_plan: Write the original output $y(t)=x^2(t)$.
Apply the system to the shifted input to get $T\{x(t-\tau)\}=x^2(t-\tau)$.
Shift the original output to get $y(t-\tau)=x^2(t-\tau)$.
Match the two expressions and state that the system preserves the input delay.
practice_variation_axes: Shift amount $\tau$
Function form of the system rule
Whether the input is given algebraically or described in words
How the matching output is written

sections.handoff_notes: The writer should show the two paths explicitly and keep the algebra minimal. The goal is the comparison, not the complexity of the system.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Preserved Delays as Time-Invariant Behavior
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that a delay preserved through the system is evidence that the system is time invariant.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the preserved-delay check is fully symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the option that correctly identifies preserved delay behavior as time invariance.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a system with delayed terms, compare the shifted-input output to the shifted original output and decide whether the delay is preserved.
distractor_plan: Match only one term and ignore the rest of the output.
Shift one side incorrectly and claim agreement.
Assume any delayed term automatically means time invariance.
Confuse preserved delay with output equality for a single input only.
Focus on the graph shape instead of the path comparison.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=x(t)+x(t-1)$ and input $x(t-\tau)$, show that the output is exactly the delayed version of the original output.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each term in the output shifts by the same amount, so the system is time invariant.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The wrinkle is that the output already contains a built-in delay, so the learner must see that the whole output still shifts by the same $\tau$.
solution_step_plan: Compute the original output $y(t)=x(t)+x(t-1)$.
Apply the system to the shifted input to get $T\{x(t-\tau)\}=x(t-\tau)+x(t-1-\tau)$.
Write the shifted original output $y(t-\tau)=x(t-\tau)+x(t-1-\tau)$.
Match the terms and conclude that the delay is preserved.
practice_variation_axes: Delay value
Number of delayed terms in the output
Whether the shift is a delay or an advance
How the matching expressions are written

sections.handoff_notes: Use a system whose output already contains delay terms so the learner sees that preserved delay is a property of the whole rule, not just of one isolated term.

sections.section_title: Rejecting Time Invariance from a Single Shifted Output
sections.learning_goal: Use the two-path test to reject time invariance when $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ does not equal $y(t-\tau)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the non-invariance decision comes from symbolic mismatch.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the option that correctly rejects time invariance by comparing the two paths.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a system with an explicit $t$ factor such as $T\{x(t)\}=t\,x(t)$, determine whether the system preserves an input delay and identify the mismatch.
distractor_plan: Treat $t$ and $t-\tau$ as interchangeable.
Assume the system is time invariant because the input was shifted.
Ignore the explicit time dependence in the system rule.
Compare only the shifted output shape and miss the algebraic mismatch.
Claim agreement after simplifying away the $\tau$ term incorrectly.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the system $T\{x(t)\}=t\,x(t)$, compare the output for $x(t-\tau)$ with $y(t-\tau)$ and show the paths do not match.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the explicit $t$ factor stays tied to the current time, so shifting the input does not simply shift the output.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This step keeps the same two-path test but switches to a time-varying rule so the mismatch is visible immediately.
solution_step_plan: Write the original output $y(t)=t\,x(t)$.
Apply the system to the shifted input to get $T\{x(t-\tau)\}=t\,x(t-\tau)$.
Shift the original output to get $y(t-\tau)=(t-\tau)\,x(t-\tau)$.
Compare the two expressions and note that they are not equal.
practice_variation_axes: The explicit time factor
The amount of input shift
Whether the mismatch is obvious from a single term or from a longer rule
The form used to state the non-invariance conclusion

sections.handoff_notes: End with a clear rejection of time invariance. The key point is the mismatch between $T\{x(t-\tau)\}$ and $y(t-\tau)$, not the mere presence of a shifted input.
